Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 97, verses 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

Page 27
[Surat al-Qadr]
Five verses, Meccan
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful
﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful
﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

First issue: The exegetes agree that what is meant is: "Indeed, We sent down the Qur'an during the Night of Decree," but God omitted the explicit mention, because this construction indicates the greatness of the Qur'an in three respects:
The first: He attributed its sending down to Himself and made it exclusive to Himself, not to anything else.
The second: He used a pronoun for it rather than its explicit name, as a testimony to its eminence and to its being independent of explicit mention. Do you not see that in the preceding surah He did not mention the name of Abu Jahl, and it was not hidden from anyone because of his fame; and His saying: ﴿Then why not, when it [the soul] reaches the throat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 83] did not mention death because of its fame? So it is here as well.
The third: the glorification of the time in which it was sent down.

Second issue: In some places He said "innī" (I), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and in some places "innā" (We), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾, ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah﴾ [Nuh: 1], ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ [al-Kawthar: 1].
Know that His saying "innā" is sometimes intended as a plural of majesty, and taking it as a plural in the sense of multiplicity is impossible, because the proofs have established the oneness of the Creator. Moreover, if there were a multiplicity of gods, the rank of each one of them would fall short of divinity, for if each of them were capable of perfection, he would be independent of each of the others, and being in need of another is a deficiency in his regard, so all would be deficient; and if none of them were capable of perfection, each would be deficient. So we know that His saying "innā" is to be understood as a plural of glorification, not a plural of number.

Third issue: If it is said: what is the meaning of His being sent down during the Night of Decree, given the knowledge that it was sent down in stages? We say there are several answers:
Page 28
The first: al-Sha'bi said: He began sending it down on the Night of Decree, because the mission began in Ramadan.
The second: Ibn Abbas said: It was sent down all at once to the lowest heaven on the Night of Decree, and then to the earth in stages, as He said: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75]. We have discussed this issue in His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. It may be asked: according to this view, why did He not say: "We sent it down to the heaven"? Because its unqualified form would suggest sending down to the earth. We reply: its sending down to the heaven is like its sending down to the earth, for He would not begin a matter and not complete it, and it is like an absent person who has come to the outskirts of a town. One says: "So-and-so has arrived," or it is said: the purpose of bringing it near and sending it down to the lowest heaven is to make them long for its descent, like one who hears the news of the arrival of a letter for his father or mother, and his longing to read it increases, as the poet said:
The longing is most intense when, one day, the homes draw near to homes.
This is because the heaven is shared between us and the angels: it is a dwelling for them and a roof and adornment for us, as He said: ﴿And We made the heaven a protected roof﴾ [al-Anbiya: 32]. So His sending down the Qur'an there is like His sending it down here.
The third answer: the intended meaning is: We sent down this Reminder ﴿during the Night of Decree﴾, i.e., in the excellence of the Night of Decree and the declaration of its nobility.

Fourth issue: al-Qadr is a verbal noun of qadirtu, aqdiru, qadran, and what is meant by it is what God executes of matters. He said: ﴿Indeed, We created everything by decree﴾ [al-Qamar: 49]. Al-qadar and al-qadr are one and the same, except that with the sukun it is a verbal noun and with the fatha it is a noun. al-Wahidi said: al-qadr in the language means "measurement," which is placing a thing on par with another without excess or deficiency. They differed about why this night was called the Night of Decree, and gave several reasons:
The first: it is the night of the determination of affairs and judgments. ʿAṭāʾ said, from Ibn Abbas: God determines what will happen in that whole year of rain, sustenance, giving life and causing death, up to the same night of the coming year. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Therein every wise matter is made distinct﴾ [al-Dukhan: 4]. Know that God's determination does not occur in that night, for He determined the measures before He created the heavens and the earth, in eternity. Rather, what is meant is the manifestation of those measures to the angels in that night by His recording them in the Preserved Tablet. This view is the choice of most scholars.
The second: It is reported from al-Zuhri that he said: the Night of Decree is the night of majesty and nobility, from the saying: "So-and-so has qadr with so-and-so," i.e., a rank and nobility. His saying supports this: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾. This may have two meanings:
One: that it refers to the agent, i.e., whoever performs acts of worship in it becomes one of rank and nobility.
Second: that it refers to the act, i.e., acts of worship have additional rank and additional nobility in that night. And from Abu Bakr al-Warraq: it was called the Night of Decree because in it was sent down a book of rank, through the tongue of an angel of rank, to a community of rank. Perhaps God mentioned the word "qadr" three times in this surah for this reason.
The third view: the Night of Decree means the night of constriction (dhiq), for the earth becomes constricted by the angels.

Fifth issue: God concealed this night for several reasons:
The first: He concealed it as He concealed all other things. He concealed His pleasure in acts of obedience, so that they would desire all of them; He concealed His anger in acts of disobedience, so that they would beware of all of them; He concealed His friend among the people, so that they would honor all of them; He concealed the answering in supplication, so that they would strive in all supplications; He concealed the Greatest Name, so that they would glorify all the names; He concealed the Middle Prayer, so that they would safeguard all of them; He concealed the acceptance of repentance, so that the responsible person would persist in all kinds of repentance; He concealed the time of death, so that the responsible person would fear. Likewise He concealed this night, so that they would glorify all the nights of Ramadan.
The second: It is as if God says: If I specified the Night of Decree, knowing your boldness in disobedience, perhaps desire would drive you in that night to disobedience, and you would fall into sin, so your disobedience with knowledge would be worse than your disobedience without knowledge. For this reason I concealed it from you. It is reported that "he (peace be upon him) entered the mosque and saw a sleeper, and said: O Ali, wake him so he may perform ablution. Ali woke him, then Ali said: O Messenger of God, you are the one who hastens to good things; why did you not wake him yourself? He said: Because his rebuking you is not disbelief, so I did this so that his offense would be lighter if he refused." If this is the mercy of the Messenger, then judge the mercy of the Lord, the Exalted by analogy. It is as if God says: If you know the Night of Decree, then if you obey in it you gain the reward of a thousand months, and if you disobey in it you gain the punishment of a thousand months, and averting punishment is preferable to acquiring reward.
The third: I concealed this night so that the responsible person would strive in seeking it, and gain the reward of striving.
The fourth: when the servant is not certain of the Night of Decree, he strives in obedience throughout all the nights of Ramadan, hoping that perhaps this night is the Night of Decree. Then God boasts of them to His angels, saying: You used to say of them that they would cause corruption and shed blood. This is their diligence and striving on the presumed night; how much more so if I made it known to him. Then the secret of His saying becomes manifest: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

Sixth issue: They differed as to whether this night entails the day. al-Sha'bi said: Yes, its day is like its night. The reason for this may be that mention of nights entails days; from this, if someone vows to observe i'tikaf for two nights, we obligate him for their two days as well. God said: ﴿And He it is who made the night and the day in succession﴾ [al-Furqan: 62], meaning the day succeeds its night and vice versa.
* * *

Seventh issue: Does this night remain? al-Khalil said: whoever says its excellence is due to the Qur'an being sent down in it says it has ceased, and it was a one-time occurrence. The majority hold that it remains. On this view, is it specific to Ramadan or not? It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: whoever stands in prayer for the whole year will attain it. Ikrimah interpreted it as the Night of Acquittal (laylat al-bara'ah) in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾ [al-Dukhan: 3]. The majority hold that it is specific to Ramadan and argue for this from His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾, so it must be that the Night of Decree is in Ramadan, lest there be contradiction. On this view they differed in specifying it in eight opinions. Ibn Razin said: the Night of Decree is the first night of Ramadan. al-Hasan al-Basri said: the seventeenth. From Anas, traced to the Prophet: the nineteenth. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: the twenty-first. From Ibn Abbas: the twenty-third. Ibn Mas'ud said: the twenty-fourth. Abu Dharr al-Ghifari said: the twenty-fifth. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and a group of the Companions said: the twenty-seventh. Some said: the twenty-ninth.

As for those who said it is the first night, they said: Wahb reported that the scrolls of Abraham were sent down on the first night of Ramadan, and the Torah six nights after the start of Ramadan, seven hundred years after the scrolls of Abraham; the Psalms were sent down to David twelve nights into Ramadan, five hundred years after the Torah; and the Gospel was sent down to Jesus eighteen nights into Ramadan, six hundred and twenty years after the Psalms. The Qur'an used to descend upon the Prophet (ﷺ) on every Night of Decree of each year: Gabriel (peace be upon him) would descend with it from the House of Majesty in the seventh heaven to the lowest heaven, so God sent down the Qur'an over twenty months in twenty years. Since this month is the one in which these great blessings occurred, it is without doubt at the peak of nobility, rank and station, so its first night was the Night of Decree. As for al-Hasan al-Basri, he said it is the night of the seventeenth, because its morning was the battle of Badr. As for the nineteenth, Anas reported a report concerning it. As for the twenty-seventh night, al-Shafi'i inclined to it because of the hadith of water and clay. What the majority hold is that it is the night of the twenty-seventh, and they mentioned for it weak indications:
The first: the hadith of Ibn Abbas that the surah has thirty words, and the word "hiya" (it) is the twenty-seventh of them.
The second: It is reported that Umar asked the Companions, then said to Ibn Abbas: "Dive in, O diver." Zayd ibn Thabit said: "You have brought the sons of the emigrants and not brought our sons." Umar said: "Perhaps you say that this is a boy, but he has what you do not have." Ibn Abbas said: "The most beloved of numbers to God Most High is the odd, and the most beloved of the odd to Him is seven," so he mentioned the seven heavens, the seven earths, the week, the levels of Hell, the number of circuits of the Tawaf, and the seven limbs; thus it indicates that it is the twenty-seventh.
The third: It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Laylat al-Qadr" has nine letters, and it is mentioned three times, making it the twenty-seventh.

Fourthly: Uthman ibn Abi al-As had a servant who said, "O my master, the water of the sea becomes sweet for one night of the month." He said, "When that night comes, inform me." It turned out to be the twenty-seventh night of Ramadan.

As for those who say it is the last night, they said: because it is the night in which the acts of worship of this month are completed. Rather, the first of Ramadan is like Adam, and its last is like Muhammad (ﷺ). For this reason it has been related in a hadith: "On the last night of Ramadan, people will be freed in number equal to those freed from the first of the month." Moreover, the first night is like the one to whom a male child is born, so it is a night of gratitude (shukr), while the last night is the night of parting, like the one whose child has died, so it is a night of patience (sabr). You have learned the difference between patience and gratitude.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ That is, your understanding does not reach the furthest extent of its virtue or the ultimate height of its rank. Then, exalted is He, He clarified its excellence in three respects.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾. On this there are several issues.

The first issue: concerning the interpretation of the verse, there are several views.

One of them: that worship in it is ﴿better than a thousand months﴾, which does not apply to this night itself. This is because it would be nearly impossible to say that it is ﴿better than a thousand months﴾ while this night itself is included in it. Rather, it is so because of the benefits, provisions and kinds of good that God increases within it.

The second: Mujahid said: There was a man among the Children of Israel who would stand in prayer through the night until morning, and then would strive (in jihad) until evening, and he did this for a thousand months. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the Muslims were amazed at this, so God revealed this verse, meaning: the Night of Decree for your community is better than a thousand months for that Israelite who bore arms for a thousand months.

The third: Malik ibn Anas said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was shown the lifespans of people, and he considered the lifespans of his community to be short, and he feared that they would not reach the same amount of deeds that the other nations had attained. So God gave him the Night of Decree, which is better than a thousand months, for all the other nations.

The fourth: al-Qasim ibn Fadl narrated from Isa ibn Mazin, who said: I said to al-Hasan ibn Ali, peace be upon him: "O you who blacken the faces of the believers! You went to this man and pledged allegiance to him," meaning Mu'awiyah. He said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw in his dream the Banu Umayyah walking over his pulpit one after another," and in another narration, "leaping upon his pulpit like monkeys." This grieved him, so God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ up to His saying: ﴿better than a thousand months﴾, meaning the rule of the Banu Umayyah. Al-Qasim said: We calculated the rule of the Banu Umayyah, and it came to a thousand months.

The judge (al-Qadi) criticized these views, saying: What has been mentioned about "a thousand months" referring to the days of the Banu Umayyah is far-fetched, because God does not describe its virtue by mentioning a thousand months of blameworthy conduct, and the days of the Banu Umayyah were blameworthy.

Know that this criticism is weak, because the days of the Banu Umayyah were great days in terms of worldly felicities, so there is nothing impossible in God saying: "I have given you a night which, in religious felicities, is better than those worldly felicities."

The second issue: this verse contains a great glad tiding and a great warning. As for the glad tiding, He, exalted is He, mentioned that this night is good, but did not specify the degree of its goodness. This is like His saying, peace be upon him: "The duel of Ali, peace be upon him, with Amr ibn Abd Wudd [al-Amiri] is better than the deeds of my community until the Day of Resurrection." He did not say "like his deed," but said "better," as if to say: "Take this as your measure, and the rest is conjecture."

Know that whoever enlivens it, it is as though he worshipped God, exalted is He, for over eighty years. Whoever enlivens it every year, it is as though he were granted many lifetimes. Whoever enlivens the month in order to attain it with certainty, it is as though he enlivened thirty nights of decree. It is related that on the Day of Resurrection there will be brought the Israelite who worshipped God for four hundred years, and there will be brought a man from this community who worshipped God for forty years, and his reward will be greater. The Israelite will say: "You are just, and I see his reward is greater." He will say: "Because you used to fear immediate punishment and so you worshipped, whereas the community of Muhammad were secure, due to His saying: ﴿And God would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. Then they worshipped, and for this reason their worship was greater in reward."

As for the warning, He, exalted is He, threatened the one who commits a major sin with entry into the Fire, and enlivening a hundred nights of Decree does not free him from that punishment deserved through the cheating of a single grain. Therefore, there is in this an indication of the magnitude of the state of sin and disobedience.

The third issue: Someone may say: It is authentically reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Your reward is according to the measure of your exertion." It is known that obedience over a thousand months is more arduous than obedience in a single night, so how can their equality be conceived? The answer is in several respects:

One: the same act may differ in its goodness and badness due to the differing circumstances attached to it. Do you not see that congregational prayer surpasses solitary prayer by so many degrees, even though the form may be broken, since the one who joins late has one rak'ah dropped from him? Also, you say of one who is being stoned: "He is being stoned because he is an adulterer," which is a good statement; but if you said it to a Christian, it would be slander requiring discretionary punishment (ta'zir); and if you said it to a married person (muhsan), it would require the prescribed penalty (hadd). So the rulings differ in these cases though the form is one in all of them. Indeed, if you said it concerning A'isha, it would be disbelief. For this reason He said: ﴿And you consider it trivial, but it is in the sight of God tremendous﴾ [al-Nur: 15]. This is because it is an attack on A'isha, who was a great transmitter of knowledge, due to his saying, peace be upon him: "Take half of your religion from this little reddish one (al-Humayra')." It is also an attack on Safwan, though he was a man of Badr; and an attack on all the believers, since she is the Mother of the Believers; and the child has the right to demand redress for slander against his mother even if he is a disbeliever. Indeed, it is an attack on the Prophet, who was the most jealous of God's creation; and indeed an attack on the wisdom of God, since it is not permissible for Him to leave him until he marries an adulteress. Then the one who says "this is an adulterer" thinks this word is easy, though it is heavier than mountains. Thus it has been established by this that acts differ in their effects regarding reward and punishment due to the differences in their aspects; so it is not far-fetched that a small act in form may be equal in reward to many acts.

The second answer: The intent of the Wise, glorified is He, is to draw creation toward acts of obedience. Sometimes He makes the reward of an act double, as He said: ﴿Indeed, with hardship there is ease. Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾ [al-Sharh: 5-6]; sometimes ten-fold, sometimes seven hundredfold; and sometimes according to times, and sometimes according to places. The essential aim of all of this is to draw the responsible person to obedience and to turn him away from preoccupation with this world. So sometimes He gives preference to the House and Zamzam over all other lands; sometimes He favors Ramadan over other months; sometimes He favors Friday over other days; and sometimes He favors the Night of Decree over other nights; and the aim is what we have mentioned.

The second point regarding the virtues of this night.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 97, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾. On this there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Know that the angels look upon spirits, and humans look upon bodies. When the angels saw your spirit as a locus for blameworthy qualities such as desire and anger, they did not accept you. They said: ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾ Your parents, when they saw the ugliness of your form at the beginning, when you were a drop of semen and a clinging clot, also did not accept you. Rather, they showed aversion, found that semen and clot disgusting, washed their clothes of it, and then strove by every means to cause its miscarriage and destruction. Then, when He, exalted is He, gave you a beautiful form, your parents, when they saw that beautiful form, accepted you and inclined toward you. Likewise, when the angels saw in your spirit the beautiful form, which is the knowledge of Allah and obedience to Him, they loved you, and they descended to you, apologizing for what they had said at first. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿The angels descend﴾. When they descend to you, they see your spirit in the darkness of the night of the body and the darkness of the bodily faculties, and then they apologize for what came before: ﴿and ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7].

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The angels descend﴾, by its apparent meaning, requires the descent of all the angels. But the angels are of immense multitude, and the earth cannot contain all of them. For this reason they differed. Some said: they descend all together to the lowest heaven. If it is objected that the difficulty remains, since the heaven is so filled that there is not a space the size of a hide without an angel in it, how can one heaven contain them all? We reply: the general meaning of the Book is given precedence over a single-transmitted report (khabar al-wahid, a report narrated by a single transmitter). Moreover, what is related is that they descend in groups, one after another, some descending and some ascending, like the people of the pilgrimage. Despite their multitude, they enter the Ka'bah entirely, yet people are between one who enters and one who leaves. For this reason the descent is extended until the rising of dawn. Therefore it is expressed with the word ﴿descend﴾ (tanazzalu), which indicates repetition, time after time.

The second opinion, which is the choice of most scholars, is that they descend to the earth. This is the more apparent, because the purpose is to encourage the revival of this night. Also, the hadiths indicate that the angels descend on all other days to gatherings of remembrance and religion, so that this occurring on this night, with its elevated status, is more fitting. Also, an unqualified descent only indicates descent from the heaven to the earth. Then those who said they descend to the earth differed in several respects:

*First:* Some said: they descend so that they may see the worship of humans, their diligence, and their striving in obedience.

*Second:* The angels said: ﴿We do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64]. This indicates that they were commanded to that descent, so it does not indicate the utmost love.

﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾: As for this verse, His saying ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾, it indicates that they first asked permission and were granted it. This indicates the utmost love, for they used to desire to come to us and long for our meeting, but they would wait for permission. If it is objected: His saying ﴿And indeed we are those who stand in ranks﴾ [As-Saffat: 165] contradicts His saying ﴿The angels descend﴾, we reply: we turn the two states to two different times.

*Third:* He, exalted is He, promised in the Hereafter that the angels would enter upon them from every gate: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 23]. Here, in this world, if you occupy yourself with My worship, the angels descend to you so that they may enter upon you to greet you and to visit. It is related from Ali, peace be upon him, that: "They descend to greet us and to intercede for us, and whoever is touched by the greeting, his sin is forgiven."

*Fourth:* Allah, exalted is He, made the virtue of this night lie in occupation with His obedience on the earth. So they descend to the earth so that their acts of obedience may be greater in reward, just as a man travels to Makkah so that his obedience there may be greater in reward. All of this is an encouragement for a person toward obedience.

*Fifth:* A person performs acts of obedience and good deeds more excellently in the presence of the great scholars and ascetics than in seclusion. So Allah, exalted is He, sent down the nearest angels, so that the one who is obligated knows that he performs acts of obedience only in the presence of those scholarly, devout, and ascetic worshippers, and thus it is more complete and further from deficiency.

*Sixth:* Some people restricted the word "angels" to some groups of angels. It is related from Ka'b that the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha) is at the limit of the seventh heaven, on the side facing Paradise. It is at the boundary of the air of this world and the air of the Hereafter. Its trunk is in Paradise, and its branches are beneath the Throne. In it are angels whose number no one knows except Allah, who worship Allah. The station of Jibril is in its midst. There is no angel among them who has not been given compassion and mercy for the believers. They descend with Jibril on the Night of Power, so no patch of the earth remains without an angel prostrating or standing upon it, supplicating for the believing men and believing women. Jibril does not leave anyone among the people without shaking his hand. The sign of this is that whoever's skin shivers, whose heart softens, and whose eyes shed tears, that is from the handshake of Jibril, peace be upon him. Whoever says in it three times: "There is no god but Allah," he is forgiven for one, delivered from the Fire by one, and admitted into Paradise by one. The first to ascend is Jibril, until he stands before the sun. He spreads out two green wings, which he does not unfurl except at that hour of that night. Then he calls one angel after another, and all of them ascend. The light of the angels and the light of Jibril's wing gather together. Jibril and those with him among the angels then stand between the sun and the lowest heaven that day, occupied with supplication, mercy, and seeking forgiveness for the believers, and for those who fasted Ramadan seeking reward. When they reach evening, they enter the lowest heaven, and they sit in circles, circle after circle. The angels of the heaven gather to them, and they ask them about man after man and woman after woman, until they say: "What did so-and-so do, and how did you find him?" They say: "We found him in the first year devoted to worship, and in this year an innovator. So-and-so was in the first year an innovator, and this year devoted to worship." Then they refrain from supplicating for the first and occupy themselves with supplicating for the second. "And we found so-and-so reciting, and so-and-so bowing, and so-and-so prostrating." They continue like this, that day and night, until they ascend to the second heaven, and so they do in every heaven until they reach the Lote Tree. Then the Lote Tree says to them: "O inhabitants of mine, tell me about the people, for I have a right over you, and I love whoever loves Allah." Ka'b related that they count for it the man and the woman by their names and their fathers' names. Then that report reaches Paradise, and Paradise says: "O Allah, hasten them to me." The angels and the people of the Lote Tree say: "Amin, amin."

When you know this, we say: whenever the gathering is greater, the descent of mercy there is greater. For this reason the greatest gatherings are at the appointed place of the Hajj, and therefore the descent of mercy there is greater. Likewise, on the Night of Power there occurs the assembly of the nearest angels, so undoubtedly the descent of mercy is greater.

* * *

**The third issue:** They mentioned several sayings about the Spirit (ar-Ruh):

*First:* It is a great angel, which, if it swallowed the heavens and the earths, would be a single morsel for it.

*Second:* A group of the angels, whom the angels see only on the Night of Power, like the ascetics whom we see only on the day of Eid.

*Third:* A creation of Allah's creation that eats and wears clothes, which are neither angels nor humans, and perhaps they are servants of the people of Paradise.

*Fourth:* It is possible that it is Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, because it is his name (the Spirit), and he descends in the company of the angels in order to look over the community of Muhammad.

*Fifth:* It is the Qur'an: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a Spirit from Our command﴾ [Ash-Shura: 52].

*Sixth:* It is mercy. It was read: ﴿and do not despair of the mercy (rawh) of Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 87] with a raised vowel (rafʿ), as if He, exalted is He, says: the angels descend, and My mercy descends in their footsteps, so they find the happiness of this world and the happiness of the Hereafter.

[Page 33]

*Seventh:* The Spirit is the most noble of the angels.

*Eighth:* From Abu Najih: the Spirits are the guardian angels and the noble scribes. The one on the right writes his doing of what is obligatory, and the one on the left writes his abstaining from what is ugly. The most correct view is that the Spirit here is Jibril. Its singling out by mention is for the increase of his nobility, as if He, exalted is He, says: the angels are on one pan, and the Spirit is on the other pan.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾, we have mentioned that this indicates that they were longing for us. If it is said: how do they desire us while knowing the abundance of our disobediences? We reply: they do not look into the details of the disobediences. It is related that they look into the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh), and they see in it the obedience of the responsible person in detail. When they reach his disobediences, the curtain is lowered, so they do not see them. Then he says: Glory be to the One who displayed the beautiful and covered the ugly.

Then, we have mentioned benefits in their descent, and we now mention other benefits. Their summary is that they see on the earth, of the kinds of acts of obedience, things they did not see in the world of the heavens:

*First:* The rich bring food from their houses and make it a feast for the poor, and the poor eat the food of the rich and worship Allah. This is a kind of obedience that does not exist in the heavens.

*Second:* They hear the moaning of the sinners, and this does not exist in the heavens.

*Third:* "Allah, exalted is He, said: 'The moaning of the sinners is more beloved to Me than the chorus of those who glorify.'" So they said: "Come, let us go to the earth and hear a voice that is more beloved to our Lord than the sound of our glorification." And how would it not be more beloved, when the chorus of those who glorify is a manifestation of the perfect state of the obedient, and the moaning of the sinners is a manifestation of the forgiving nature of the Lord of the earth and the heavens? [And this is the first issue.]

**The second issue:** This verse indicates the infallibility ('ismah) of the angels. Its parallels are His saying: ﴿And We do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64], and His saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 27]. There is a subtle point in it: He, exalted is He, did not say "permitted," but said: ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾, which is an indication that they do not act in any way except with His permission. From this is the saying of a man to his wife: "If you go out except with my permission," for the permission is required for every going out.

**The third issue:** His saying: ﴿their Lord﴾ conveys the glorification of the angels and the belittling of the sinners, as if He, exalted is He, said: "They were Mine, so I was theirs." Its parallel regarding us is: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yunus: 3]. And He said to Muhammad, peace be upon him: ﴿When your Lord said﴾ [Sad: 71]. Its parallel is what is related: when Dawud (David) fell ill with his final illness, he said: "My God, be for Sulayman as You were for me." So the revelation descended: "Say to Sulayman: let him be for Me as you were for Me." It is also related from Ibrahim the Friend, peace be upon him, that he lacked a guest for several days, so he went out with a food-bag (sufrah) to seek a guest. Then he found a tent, and he called out: "Do you want a guest?" It was said: "Yes." So he said to the host: "Is there with you a condiment of milk or honey?" The man lifted two rocks and struck one against the other, and they split. From one of them came milk, and from the other honey. Ibrahim wondered and said: "My God, I am Your friend, and I have not found such honor. What is his [status]?" Then the revelation descended: "O My friend, he was for Us, so We were for him."

* *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from every matter (min kulli amr)﴾, its meaning is: the angels and the Spirit descend therein on account of every matter, and the meaning is that each one of them descended for another matter. Then they mentioned about it several aspects:

*First:* They are occupied with many affairs: some with bowing, some with prostration, some with supplication, and likewise with reflection, teaching, and conveying the revelation; and some for attaining the virtue of the night, or to greet the believers.

Secondly: this is the view of most scholars, that it is "on account of every matter" (min ajli kulli amrin) that has been decreed in that year, whether good or evil. In this there is an indication that their descent is an act of worship, as though they were saying: "We did not descend to the earth out of the desires of our own souls, but for every matter in which there is benefit for the responsible servants (al-mukallafin)." The word "amr" is general so that it includes the good of this world and the Hereafter, a clarification from Him that they descend with what is the welfare of the responsible servant in his religion and his worldly life. It is as if a questioner says, "From where have you come?" and the answer is, "What concern is this of yours, this meddling? Rather, say: for what matter have you come? Because it is your share."

Thirdly: some read it as "min kulli im'ri'" (from every man), meaning on account of every person. It is narrated that they do not meet any believing man or believing woman without greeting them. It was said: Is it not narrated that the lives (al-ajal) and provisions (al-arzaq) are apportioned on the night of the middle of Sha'ban, and now you say that this occurs on the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr)? We say: It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed Allah decrees the decrees on the Night of Acquittal (laylat al-bara'a), then when the Night of Power comes He hands them over to their owners." It was also said: On the Night of Acquittal He decrees the lives and provisions, and on the Night of Power He decrees the matters in which there is good, blessing and safety. It was also said: On the Night of Power He decrees what concerns the honouring (i'zaz) of the religion and what has great benefit for the Muslims. As for the Night of Acquittal, the names of those who will die are written in it and they are handed over to the Angel of Death (malak al-mawt).

**Third aspect: on the virtues of this night.** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Peace it is until the rising of dawn﴾. On this there are several issues.

**First issue: on His saying ﴿peace﴾, there are several interpretations.**

First: the night of Qadr, until the rising of dawn, is peace, meaning that the angels greet the obedient with peace. This is because the angels descend in groups, one after another, from the beginning of the night until the rising of dawn, so the descent follows in succession because of the abundance of greetings of peace.

Second: the night is described as peace. Then this peace should not be considered small, for seven angels greeted Abraham, the Friend (al-Khalil), in the story of the roasted calf. His joy at that exceeded his joy at possessing the world. Indeed, when the angels greeted him with peace, the fire of Nimrod became for him ﴿coolness and peace﴾ [al-Anbiya: 69]. Will not His fire, by the blessing of the angels' greeting of peace upon us, become coolness and peace? However, Abraham's hospitality to them was a roasted calf, while they want from us a roasted heart. Moreover, there is a subtle point in it, which is showing the excellence of this Ummah: there the angels descended upon Abraham, and here they descended upon the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Third: it is peace from evils and calamities, meaning safety. This is like saying: "So-and-so is hajj and ghazw," meaning he is always occupied with them. A similar example is the verse:

*"For it is only coming and going."*

It is said that in the night of Qadr the angels and the Spirit descend with good things and felicities, and no harm is decreed in it. Therefore whatever descends in this night is peace, meaning safety, benefit and good.

Fourth: Abu Muslim (al-Isfahani) said: "Peace" means the night is safe from winds, harm, thunderbolts, and whatever resembles these.

Fifth: it is peace in which Satan cannot do any evil.

Sixth: the pause is at His saying ﴿from every matter, peace﴾, so that the word "peace" connects with what precedes it, and its meaning is that the decree of good, blessing and safety continues until the rising of dawn. This interpretation is weak.

[p. 36]

Seventh: from its beginning until the rising of dawn it is safe in that worship in each of its parts is better than a thousand months. It is not like other nights in that the first third is recommended for obligatory prayer, half for voluntary worship, and the pre-dawn hours for supplication. Rather, all its times and parts are equal.

Eighth: "Peace it is" means "it is Paradise", because among the names of Paradise is "the Abode of Peace" (dar al-salam), meaning Paradise formed from safety.

**Second issue: al-matla' (المَطْلَع) means al-tulu' (الطُّلُوع, the rising).** It is said: "The dawn rose (talaʿa al-fajr) with tuluʿan and matlaʿan." The meaning is that this peace continues until the rising of dawn. Whoever reads it with a kasra on the lam (مَطْلِع) takes it as a noun for the time of rising. Likewise, the place of rising is also called maṭlaʿ, as said by al-Zajjaj. As for Abu Ubayda, al-Farra' and others, they preferred a fatha on the lam (مَطْلَع) because it has the meaning of the verbal noun (masdar). They said: the kasra form is a noun like al-mashriq (the place of sunrise), and there is no sense in a noun for the place of rising here. However, if it is understood as al-Zajjaj mentioned, as a noun for the time of rising, it is correct. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: it is possible to understand it as a verbal noun as well, because among verbal nouns that should be of the form maf'il is what has been given a kasra, like their saying: ʿalaʾ al-makbir and al-maʿjiz. Compare His saying: ﴿And they ask you about menstruation﴾ [al-Baqara: 222]. Likewise, the kasra in maṭliʿ came as an anomaly from what its pattern requires.

And Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows best, and may Allah bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
